blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better value for US and European residential scraping: $35 for 10 GB against $50 on SOAX Sandbox for US traffic, about $200 for 100 GB against $300 on SOAX Builder, and no credit expiry. SOAX is the better choice for mobile-first work, ad verification and multi-country campaigns, where its 33M mobile IPs, ISP-level targeting on every plan and UDP, QUIC and SOCKS5 support matter, and its Tier 3 country rates can undercut Rayobyte.

SOAX and Rayobyte take nearly opposite approaches to residential pricing. Rayobyte sells simple volume bands where traffic never expires and the rate falls to $0.90/GB at a terabyte. SOAX sells prepaid credits that expire after 60 days, with a per-GB rate set by your plan and the exit country's tier. SOAX also runs a large mobile network on the same balance and supports SOCKS5, UDP and QUIC, while Rayobyte's residential gateway is HTTP(S) only. Here is how to choose.

blocks.text: SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX rebuilt its pricing in 2026 around credits and country tiers. Residential and mobile traffic share one balance and one per-GB rate, and the rate depends on your plan and the country your exit IP is in: US and German traffic costs more than Indian or Filipino traffic. SOAX advertises 155 million residential and 33 million mobile IPs in 195 countries, supports UDP and QUIC as well as SOCKS5, and includes city and ISP targeting on every plan. It discontinued its datacenter and ISP proxies between late 2025 and mid 2026.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: SOAX vs Rayobyte

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

At 10 GB a month, Rayobyte is the cheaper option at about $35 against $50 for SOAX, roughly 30% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $200 with Rayobyte and $300 with SOAX: a 33% saving in Rayobyte's favour. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while SOAX's allowance does not (credits expire 60 days after they are added). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. SOAX lists '155M residential + 33M mobile' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, SOAX lists 195 countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. SOAX supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, UDP, QUIC, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in SOAX's favour. On sessions, SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. With Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. Run the same small test on both before committing.
SERP and rank tracking: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: city and ISP targeting for local results. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: granular location filters. With Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: fewer carrier or ASN controls.
Tight budgets: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. How SOAX compares: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test SOAX and Rayobyte before you commit
The quickest way to choose between SOAX and Rayobyte is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, SOAX comes out ahead in 3, Rayobyte in 1, and 2 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
